tagline: Peninsula hills screen a freeway beside the San Andreas rift valley.
intro: Interstate 280 runs along the Peninsula hills, with the Santa Cruz Mountains to the west and views of San Francisco Bay at a few points to the east. Much of this stretch follows the eastern rim of the San Andreas Fault’s rift valley. Caltrans designates the section from the San Mateo–Santa Clara county line to the San Bruno city limits as a scenic highway, recognizing a landscape without visual intrusions.

The San Jose–San Francisco route joined the Interstate Highway System in 1955. Construction came in stages: the Cupertino–Woodside section was completed in the late 1960s, while the section between SR 92 and SR 84 waited until the 1970s. Until then, traffic used Cañada Road between the completed ends. The Doran Memorial Bridge opened in 1969, carrying the freeway across the creek gorge beside the 1888 Crystal Springs Dam.

Heading south from San Bruno, the freeway leaves its urban setting for the hills west of the Peninsula cities. Between Hillsborough and Belmont, it overlooks Crystal Springs Reservoir and crosses San Mateo Creek on the Doran Memorial Bridge. Farther south, near Sand Hill Road, SLAC’s two-mile linear accelerator passes 30 feet beneath the highway. Near the southern end of this county segment, Ladera occupies the bottom of the mountains’ eastern slope, beside Alpine Road.
notice: Between Hillsborough and Belmont, Crystal Springs Reservoir occupies part of the fault’s rift valley.

moments.title: Crystal Springs Rest Area
moments.text: A 26-foot statue of Junípero Serra once stood at Crystal Springs Rest Area, visible from both directions on I-280. The freeway’s Serra name was established by a 1967 legislative resolution honoring the Spanish missionary who founded California missions in the eighteenth century. Installed in 1975, the faux-sandstone figure was removed by Caltrans in 2025. Caltrans said the installation failed to meet current Transportation Art Program requirements and had repeatedly attracted graffiti and vandalism. The rest area is on northbound I-280, north of the Doran Memorial Bridge; markers there commemorate Eugene A. Doran and the bridge’s steel-design award.

moments.title: Doran Memorial Bridge
moments.text: Four concrete piers with modified Gothic arches support the twin steel girder bridges over San Mateo Creek. During construction, workers lowered materials from a high line between towers on the adjoining cliffs to reduce disturbance to the gorge. Before the May 1969 opening ceremony, more than 30,000 people crossed on foot during Pedestrian Day. Named for Hillsborough police officer Eugene A. Doran in 1969, the bridge was rededicated in 2004 to include his son Patrick, a Marine who died in Vietnam. Slanted side panels conceal the structural steel, and the concrete piers were contoured to help the bridge fit its surroundings.

moments.title: Ladera
moments.text: Ladera’s name means hillside in Spanish, and its streets carry Spanish phrases or botanical names. The community lies at the bottom of the Santa Cruz Mountains’ eastern slope, bordered by Alpine Road to the east and Stanford’s Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve to the west. The land became part of the Macdonough family’s Ormondale Ranch in 1927, where they raised cattle and sheep and bred racehorses. In 1946, members of the Peninsula Housing Association bought the ranch’s remaining 260 acres for a housing cooperative. They chose landscape architect Garrett Eckbo to lay out the community and architects Joseph Allen Stein and John Funk to design early model homes.
